title: Modern Orthodoxy
hookLine: full halakha joined with engagement in the wider world

cards: Six in the morning, a hospital stairwell. A resident in green scrubs, at the end of a long night shift, has a small prayer book open against the railing.
She's saying the morning prayers before rounds, between the vending machine and the fire door. In an hour she'll present cases to her attending. Tonight she'll light Shabbat candles.
Nothing in her day is split into a religious half and a worldly half. She'd say it's one life. Today, the stream that tries to live that way.

teach.b: Modern Orthodoxy. Full halakha, and the whole world too. First, the law is not lighter.

Modern Orthodox Jews keep Shabbat, keep kosher, pray, and hold the Torah as given by God, just as yesterday's communities do. The difference isn't how much of the law, but how open the door to the wider world is.
Second, an old line. In the tractate of the Fathers, Rabban Gamliel teaches that Torah study is excellent when joined with derekh eretz, a worldly occupation, the way of the land.
Torah without work, he says, ends up empty. Third, a modern teacher. Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik, a Modern Orthodox thinker, read the first chapters of Genesis as two portraits of one person.

The first Adam is told to "replenish the earth, and subdue it": build, discover, master the world. The second Adam is placed in the garden "to dress it and to keep it": to serve, to belong, to stand before God.
A person of faith, he taught, is called to be both, and the two never fully settle. Fourth, what that looks like. Secular university next to the study hall.
Science next to Talmud. A career, a vote, a seat at the table of public life, and a full Shabbat.

teach.h: TORAH WITH THE WAY OF THE LAND.
teach.b: Some call it Torah and worldly knowledge; some, Torah with the way of the land.
And it carries real tensions, which its own thinkers argue about openly: how far to engage, and where to hold the line.
The resident in the stairwell holds both books.

teach.h: TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.
teach.b: Modern Orthodoxy says that's the point.

how: Modern Orthodox Jews keep halakha in full while studying and working in the wider world, often in schools that teach Jewish texts alongside secular subjects.

o: full Jewish law joined with life in the wider world
a newer, lighter Orthodoxy that keeps less of the law
the Orthodox churches of Eastern Europe today

s: Modern Orthodox Jews keep a lighter version of the law

games.q: Genesis gives two portraits of the first human. which does Soloveitchik say a person of faith should choose?
o: the first: build and master the world.
the second: serve and stand before God.
both, in one person, never fully settled.
games.why: both. he read the two Adams as one person, called to build the world and to serve before God, with the tension never fully resolved.

practice: Bring to mind the next real task waiting for you, an email, a shift, a class, the dishes, and take one of today's lines into it: to dress it and to keep it, to serve the thing in front of you, not only to master it.
Picture yourself doing it that way, with care, start to finish. If you pray, you can hold the task up in that prayer.

wordCard.voice: Modern Orthodoxy. Full halakha joined with engagement in the wider world: Torah with the way of the land, two Adams in one person. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Torah with the way of the land, Torah joined with worldly life, from the tractate of the Fathers.

carryVoice: Your line: torah and the world. One life, not two halves stitched together. Until tomorrow.
